# 2 Samuel Chapter 14 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 183v–184v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_014_page_001.jpg, 2SA_014_page_002.jpg, 2SA_014_page_003.jpg

---

**1** Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king's heart was set on Absalom.

**2** So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman. He said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but be as a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead.

**3** Then go to the king and speak to him in this manner." And Joab put the words in her mouth.

**4** When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and bowed down and said, "Save me, O king!"

**5** The king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She said, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead.

**6** Your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field, and there was no one to separate them, and the one struck the other and killed him.

**7** Now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the one who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed, and so destroy the heir as well.' Thus they would quench my last remaining ember, and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth."

**8** The king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you."

**9** The woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless."

**10** The king said, "If anyone speaks to you, bring him to me, and he shall not touch you again."

**11** Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood not destroy further, lest they destroy my son." He said, "As the LORD lives, not a hair of your son shall fall to the ground."

**12** Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."

**13** The woman said, "Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this verdict the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring back his own banished one.

**14** We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away life; rather, he devises plans so that the banished one may not remain an outcast from him.

**15** Now I have come to speak this word to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid. Your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; perhaps the king will grant the request of his servant.

**16** For the king will hear, and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the inheritance of God.'

**17** And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. May the LORD your God be with you."

**18** Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." The woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."

**19** The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; he put all these words in the mouth of your servant.

**20** In order to change the course of affairs, your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God, to know all things that are on the earth."

**21** Then the king said to Joab, "Behold, I grant this. Go, bring back the young man Absalom."

**22** And Joab fell on his face to the ground and bowed down and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant."

**23** So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.

**24** But the king said, "Let him turn to his own house, but let him not see my face." So Absalom turned to his own house and did not see the king's face.

**25** Now in all Israel there was no man so praised for his beauty as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.

**26** And when he cut the hair of his head — at the end of every year he used to cut it, for it was heavy on him — he weighed the hair of his head: two hundred shekels by the king's weight.

**27** There were born to Absalom three sons and one daughter, whose name was Tamar. She was a woman beautiful in appearance.

**28** So Absalom lived in Jerusalem two full years without seeing the king's face.

**29** Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. He sent a second time, but he would not come.

**30** Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.

**31** Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"

**32** Absalom answered Joab, "Look, I sent word to you, saying, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would have been better for me to remain there."' Now therefore let me see the king's face, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death."

**33** Then Joab went to the king and told him. And he summoned Absalom, and he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king. And the king kissed Absalom.

---
## LOGOS Translation Notes

**Verse 1 — "perceived":** The Hebrew *vayeda'* means "knew/perceived." Joab reads David's emotional state with the same shrewdness he applies to everything. The phrase *lev ha-melekh al Avshalom* — "the heart of the king was upon Absalom" — expresses David's longing, which Joab discerns and exploits.

**Verse 7 — "my last remaining ember":** The Hebrew *gachalti* (my coal/ember) is one of the most poignant metaphors in the Old Testament for the survival of a family line. A single glowing coal can rekindle a fire; to quench it is to extinguish the family forever.

**Verse 14 — theological center:** The woman's speech contains a remarkable theological argument: (1) all humans die (*mot namut*); (2) death is irreversible, like water spilled on the ground; (3) yet God does not simply take away life — he devises means (*machashavot*) to restore the banished. The implication: if God acts to bring back the exiled, should not the king?

**Verse 17 — "angel of God":** The comparison of the king to the *mal'akh ha-elohim* attributes to the king a quasi-divine capacity for discernment. The same phrase is used of David in 1 Sam 29:9. Here it serves the woman's rhetorical purpose but also carries genuine theological weight about the nature of royal authority.

**Verse 24 — partial restoration:** David's command creates a painful half-measure: Absalom may return to Jerusalem but may not see the king's face. This incomplete reconciliation — presence without relationship — will fester for two more years and contribute directly to the rebellion of chapter 15.

**Verse 27 — "Tamar":** Absalom names his daughter after his violated sister. The act preserves her memory and signals that the wound remains open. The narrator's observation that this Tamar was also beautiful echoes the description of her aunt in 13:1 — beauty within David's house continues to be both gift and vulnerability.

**Consistent terms:** Joab (Yo'av), Absalom (Avshalom), the LORD (YHWH), banished one (niddach), inheritance (nachalah).

*— LOGOS*
